content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, specifically focusing on tests for TB infection. These guidelines, published in 2022, aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the use of various diagnostic tools, including tuberculin skin tests (TSTs), interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), and newer Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs). The guidelines are intended for policymakers, clinicians, laboratory specialists, and other stakeholders involved in TB and HIV programs, particularly in resource-limited settings. The guidelines emphasize that approximately one-quarter of the global population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Testing for TB infection is critical to identifying individuals who may benefit from TB preventive treatment (TPT). However, there is no gold-standard test for diagnosing TB infection. The currently available tests, TSTs and IGRAs, are indirect methods that rely on the immune response to detect TB infection. A positive result from either test does not reliably predict the risk of progression to active TB disease. In 2011, WHO issued recommendations on the use of IGRAs for diagnosing TB infection. These included technologies such as the tuberculin skin test (TST), QIAGEN QuantiFERON®-TB Gold (QFT-G), QIAGEN QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT), and Oxford Immunotec T-SPOT®.TB (T-SPOT). In 2018, WHO updated its recommendations, stating that either TST or IGRAs (or both) could be used for TB infection diagnosis. This recommendation was included in the WHO consolidated guidelines on TB prevention, specifically in Module 1: Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment. In 2021, WHO extended its recommendations to include newer technologies such as Beijing Wantai’s TB-IGRA and QIAGEN QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus. Additionally, newer TBSTs, which use specific Mtb antigens like ESAT-6 and CFP-10, have been developed. These tests combine the simplicity of skin-test platforms with the specificity of IGRAs. Emerging evidence suggests that TBSTs may have similar specificity to IGRAs and provide more reliable results in children, adolescents, and people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, this evidence has not been systematically reviewed. In 2022, WHO issued recommendations on the use of TBSTs for diagnosing TB infection. The evaluated technologies included Cy-Tb (Serum Institute of India), Diaskintest® (Generium, Russian Federation), and C-TST (formerly known as ESAT-6-CFP-10 test, Anhui Zhifei Longcom, China). The objectives of the guidelines were to assess the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of TSTs, IGRAs, and TBSTs; evaluate their concordance; and analyze their impact on patient outcomes, such as the efficacy of TPT based on diagnostic test results and predictive value for progression to active TB disease. The guidelines also reviewed qualitative data on the feasibility, accessibility, equity, and end-user values related to the implementation of these tests, as well as economic data on affordability, cost, and cost-effectiveness. The systematic reviews followed detailed protocols with predefined questions relevant to the individual topics. The recommendations include the following: 1. Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) may be used to test for TB infection. This is a conditional recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 2. Either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) can be used to test for TB infection. This is a strong recommendation with very low certainty of evidence. 3. IGRAs and TSTs should not be used in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) for diagnosing pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB or for the diagnostic work-up of adults (including PLHIV) suspected of active TB in these settings. This is a strong recommendation. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) concluded that the diagnostic accuracy of TBSTs is similar to that of IGRAs and greater than that of TSTs. However, concerns were raised about the quality of evidence and the lack of longitudinal studies evaluating the impact of these tests on patient-important outcomes. The risk of bias was noted, particularly from non-blinded studies, and the quantity and quality of evidence varied among the different tests. For two of the three evaluated TBSTs (Diaskintest and C-TST), evidence on specificity was generated in high TB burden settings. Additional analyses considered the concordance in specificity with existing WHO-recommended IGRAs. All three evaluated TBSTs have the potential to be used for detecting TB infection and are recommended. In summary, the WHO guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for the use of diagnostic tests for TB infection, highlighting the strengths and limitations of each method. The recommendations aim to improve TB control efforts, particularly in resource-limited settings, by guiding the selection and implementation of appropriate diagnostic tools.
